world.org_type: nonprofit regional health system with three hospitals and an employed medical group, replacing commercial occurrence professional liability policies with a self-insured claims-made trust

driver: A cover that pays only for events first reported inside its own short window is priced as the count of past events that would report in time at the average cost of all past events, when a past event's cost depends on how soon it was reported, and not in one direction: the quickest reports are costly, the next quickest cheap and the late ones carry most of the money; the expected cost is each past event's own cost counted for the exposure from which its own delay still lands it inside the window, which neither the average cost, the average cost of the events reported within a period nor a smooth curve of cost on delay gives.
driver_concrete: Each hospital and the employed medical group joins the new trust, claims-made, on the day its occurrence policy expires, so the 2027 cost is the Claims first made by 31 December 2027 from incidents after each entity's Transition Date; in the system's 2016 to 2024 experience the Claims made within weeks are disclosed harm the Early Resolution Program settles at tens of thousands, those made in the following months mostly program requests settled for a few thousand, and the demands and suits made a year or more on carry nearly all the cost, so the window's expected cost is each experience Claim's own trended cost counted for the covered FTE-years of 2027 with its own delay still left, within its specialty class, not the window's expected count at the class's average cost, at the average cost of the Claims made within a year, or along a fitted severity curve.
stump: A competent solver who reads the claims-made window correctly counts the Claims the 2016 to 2024 experience would make by 31 December 2027 from each entity's Transition Date and prices them at each specialty class's average trended Claim cost (frequency times severity), filing $2,500,000 ($2,605,268 unrounded); the step that lands it there is pricing the window's Claims at the cost of all Claims, when the Claims made inside a first claims-made year are the disclosed-harm settlements made within weeks (about $54,500 each in the experience) and the program requests made months later (about $8,600 each), while the average carries the demands and suits made a year or more later (about $443,000 each); costing each experience Claim at its own delay against each entity's days in the trust gives $1,250,000.
analyst_test: a strong analyst who dedupes the register, merges each incident's claim numbers, reads the claims-made window and counts the expected Claims made by 31 December 2027 from each Transition Date correctly still prices them at each specialty class's average Claim cost and files $2,500,000; a severity from the Claims made within a year gives $750,000, a log-linear severity curve on the delay $1,000,000, a lognormal or gamma log-delay severity $1,500,000; only costing each Claim at its own delay (or in delay bands fine enough to part the weeks from the months) lands $1,250,000.
domain_test: the deciding quantity is the expected cost of claims first made inside a claims-made trust's opening window, built from each entity's covered exposure through the system's own report-lag experience with each claim's cost tied to its own report lag, which is how a professional liability actuary prices a first claims-made year; with another field's nouns (a warranty, a subscription) there is no claims-made trigger, retroactive date, early-resolution settlement or late suit for the cost to depend on.

differentiation.task102: task102 moves payments across a period boundary by a business-day release rule; here nothing moves across a boundary: a claims-made window keeps only the claims made soon after their incident, which are the cheap early-resolution ones, so the cost is the exposure at each point of each entity's months of cover times the cost of past claims made within the time then left.
differentiation.task501: task501 v3 sized a buffer on the furthest a cumulative path ran ahead of its forecast inside a test horizon; here no path maximum or buffer is involved: the cost of a claims-made opening window is a lag-truncated, cost-weighted share of exposure, entity by entity.
differentiation.task134: task134 v2 round 2 forecasts a pool's inflow over a window holding an announced threshold step, the step's size scaled from a smaller one the history holds; here no threshold steps and nothing is scaled: a claims-made opening window keeps only the claims made soon after their incident, the cheap early-resolution ones, so the cost is each day's covered exposure times the trended cost of past claims made within the days then left.
differentiation.task130: v4 round 1's decisive step was the claims-made window itself (truncating each claim's report lag against each entity's days in the trust, against a mature year's cost per FTE-year); here that truncation is the default path's own construction and the decisive step is the cost each window claim carries: the experience's cost is non-monotone in the report lag and class-specific, so the window's expected count at the average claim cost, a within-a-year severity and a fitted severity curve all miss, and only costing each claim at its own lag lands.

lineage.driver: Members of a closed group leave only when a rationed supply reaches them, and the supply is handed out across a wider list in a filed priority order within each size class, so how many remain at a later date is each member's rank inside its class against the cumulative planned supply, and neither a leaving rate nor a survival curve read off history, which both average over whatever list length the past happened to have, gives it.

lineage.driver: A cover whose first window sees only the events reported soon after they occur is priced on a history in which only some units ran the process that produces those quick, cheap reports, while every unit runs it from the window's start; the window's cost is carried almost entirely by the quick events that only the process's units show, so the history pooled across every unit about halves it, and the process's effect read over a full period of development, where it makes the units look cheaper, points the wrong way; the window is costed at each point of its exposure on the experience of the units that already ran the process, one rate for every unit.
